A harmony wheel, a WCAG contrast checker, tonal palettes, vision simulation and more — every tool runs on the same engine the lessons teach.
Chromatic holds no internet permission — Android itself prevents it from going online. No accounts, no analytics, no tracking. Crash reports stay on your device unless you share them.
One payment, everything included, free updates. And Theme Studio can re-theme this very app from a single color — try it first.
Why hues live on a circle — and how that one shape unlocks every harmony rule you\'ll ever use.

In 1666 Isaac Newton bent light through a prism and arranged the resulting colors in a circle, inventing the color wheel. Artists later built the traditional Red-Yellow-Blue (RYB) wheel for paint, while screens use Red-Green-Blue (RGB) light and printers use Cyan-Magenta-Yellow (CMY) ink. The model changes the exact hues, but the wheel\'s job is always the same: it is a map of relationships.

Primary colors can\'t be mixed from others. Secondaries sit halfway between two primaries, and tertiaries between a primary and a secondary. The positions matter more than the names: colors directly opposite each other are complements, and neighbors are family.
The color family itself — what makes red \'red\' regardless of how light, dark, or dull it is.
The hue directly opposite on the wheel; mixing complements produces neutrals.
Every color has three dials. Master them and you can generate thousands of controlled variations instead of guessing.

Hue is which color it is (0–360°). Saturation is how intense vs. gray it is. Lightness (or Value) is how much white or black it contains. HSL and HSV are just two slightly different ways of turning those dials into RGB numbers.

A tint adds white (lighter), a shade adds black (darker), and a tone adds gray (duller). Professional design systems are built on tonal scales — one hue stepped through many lightness levels — because they guarantee every combination stays in the same family.
Muted (low-saturation) palettes read as calm and professional.
Extreme lightness contrast creates hierarchy without new hues.
Screens work in RGB, but humans reason in HSL — convert constantly.
Harmonies are recipes for combining hues so they look intentional instead of accidental.

Complementary pairs maximize contrast; analogous trios minimize it; triadic, split-complementary, and tetradic schemes live in between. Monochromatic drops hue variety entirely and varies lightness. Each recipe answers a different question: do you want tension, calm, or richness?

A harmony is not a democracy. Give roughly 60% of a design to your dominant color, 30% to the secondary, and 10% to the accent. The accent — often the complement — earns its punch precisely because it is rare. Equal shares of contrasting colors look loud and unresolved.
Color doesn\'t exist in isolation. Neighbors, warmth, and expectation all bend what the eye reports.

The exact same gray looks darker on white and lighter on black, and a color\'s hue is judged relative to its surroundings. This is why colors must always be evaluated in context — a palette that works in swatches can fail in a layout.
Reds, oranges, and yellows feel closer and more urgent; blues and greens feel farther and calmer. Designers exploit this: warm colors for calls to action, cool colors for backgrounds and structure.
Colors carry associations — but they are statistical tendencies, not laws. Context and culture decide.

Red signals urgency, appetite, and error. Blue reads as trustworthy and calm — hence banks. Green suggests growth, health, and success. Yellow is optimistic but fatigues at scale. Purple implies luxury or creativity. Black is premium; white is clean.

Associations shift across cultures (white mourns in parts of Asia) and across context (red is \'sale\' in retail but \'error\' in software). The reliable strategy: pick associations that match your product, then validate with real users — never rely on color alone to carry meaning.
WCAG turns \'is this readable?\' into numbers you can verify — and your tools can automatically fix.

WCAG computes relative luminance from each color\'s linearized RGB channels, then takes the ratio between the lighter and darker color plus 0.05. The result spans 1:1 (identical) to 21:1 (black on white). Because luminance is nonlinear, two mid-greys can fail even when they look different.

Body text needs 4.5:1 for AA and 7:1 for AAA. Large text (≈18pt bold / 24pt) needs 3.0:1. UI components and graphical objects need 3.0:1 against adjacent colors. And never encode meaning in color alone — pair it with icons, labels, or patterns.
Perceived brightness of a color on a 0–1 scale, weighted for human vision (green dominates).
How the theory becomes a shipped app: semantic roles, tonal scales, dark mode, and restraint.

Design systems assign colors to roles — primary, on-primary, surface, surface-variant, error — and components reference the roles. That abstraction is what makes themes, dark mode, and Material You dynamic color possible: swap the role mapping, keep the components.

Dark themes are not inverted photos: keep the hue, invert the lightness ramp, and use slightly desaturated tones to avoid vibration on dark surfaces. Limit a screen to one accent-worthy moment; if everything is emphasized, nothing is.
